favour noun

a kindness done

also favor, do someone a favour, ask a favour, as a favour, a good turn, kindness (a kind act), do me a favour, please do me this favour, ask someone for a favour, return a favour, do someone a big favour

classical

Ter. Ad. 254: beneficium accipere (Lewis & Short, as Ad. 2.3.1)
Cic. Off. 1.48: beneficium dare (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 313
Traupman 336
Traupman 152, 399

beneficium, beneficiī n.

noun, second declension

a kindness, a good turn

A service one was free not to render; one owed by family or by station is an officium (Sen. Ben. 3.18.1, quoted by Lewis & Short). beneficium dare, accipere, reddere; beneficiō tuō, thanks to you.

Other words

  • grātum facere — do (someone) a favour

    phrase: alicui grātum (grātissimum) facere · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 2.19.2; Cic. Fam. 3.9.2; Ter. Eun. 4.4.56 (Lewis & Short), s.v. faciō; Traupman 98: grātum alicui facere; Traupman 313

    The polite request of Cicero’s letters: grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī …, “you will do me the greatest favour if …”. A plain “please” is sī mē amās (Cic. Fam. 9.20.3).

  • officium, officiī n. — a service, a good office

    noun, second declension · also used · classical

    A kindness done for someone who has a claim to it, as a friend or kinsman has (Lewis & Short); its other common sense is duty.

  • grātia, grātiae f. — a favour asked or granted

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plaut. Capt. 3.5.63: ab eō petītō grātiam istam (Lewis & Short); Traupman 98: grātiam ab aliquō petere; Traupman 313

    Rare in this sense (Lewis & Short); its everyday senses are goodwill (see favour, goodwill) and, in the plural, thanks.

  • Fac hanc grātiam mihi. — given for “please do me this favour”

    avoid · modern · Traupman 98: please do me this favor, amābō tē, fac hanc grātiam mihi; Traupman 313

    Grātiam facere is classically to let someone off a fault or an obligation, to pardon (dēlictī grātiam facere, Sall. Jug. 104, Lewis & Short s.v. grātia; see forgive). To ask a favour, say amābō tē with the imperative, or grātum mihi fēceris, sī … (above); Terence has hanc grātiam ut sibi dēs, that you grant him this favour (Ter. Hec. 3.3.30, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī ad mē in Ciliciam quam prīmum vēneris

    you will do me the greatest favour if you come to me in Cilicia as soon as you canCic. Fam. 2.19.2

  • Inopī beneficium bis dat, quī dat celeriter.

    He does the needy a double kindness who does it quickly.Publ. I 6

  • Optimē positum est beneficium, ubi ejus meminit quī accipit.

    A kindness is best placed where the one who receives it remembers it.Publ. O 26

  • beneficium accipere et reddere

    to accept and return a favourTraupman 152

  • grātissimum alicui facere

    to do someone a big favourTraupman 313

  • grātiam alicui referre

    to return someone a favourTraupman 313

See also favour, help, thank you, kind, in exchange for, forgive.
